*A cheap way to tidy up a snake, and why the hard part is somewhere else.*

---

## A game on the corners of a cube

Take an ordinary cube and label its eight corners with three-bit strings: $000$, $001$, $010$, and so on up to $111$. Two corners share an edge exactly when their labels differ in one bit. Do the same thing with $n$ bits and you get the **$n$-dimensional hypercube** $Q_n$. It has $2^n$ corners, and each corner has $n$ neighbours, one for each bit you can flip.

Now play a game. Start at some corner and walk along edges. Each step flips one bit. There is one rule, and it is strict: **your path may never come back next to itself.** Each new corner you step on must be adjacent to the corner you just left and to no other corner you have already visited. A path that follows this rule is called a **snake**, and the old puzzle known as *snake-in-the-box* asks how long a snake can get.

The rule bites quickly. In the ordinary cube $Q_3$ the longest snake has just $4$ edges, although the cube has $8$ corners. The best known lengths grow like this:

| dimension $n$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| longest snake $S(n)$ | 1 | 2 | 4 | 7 | 13 | 26 | 50 |

After $n = 7$ nobody knows the exact answer, and record-hunters use large computer searches to push the lower bounds up. The question has a practical side as well. A snake is a code that detects errors. If you read a sequence of positions from a sensor and a single bit is corrupted, the corrupted word is either not a position on the snake or sits right next to the true one, so the damage stays small. Engineers met this problem in the 1950s while designing analog-to-digital converters, and it has stayed in the literature since.

The obvious difficulty is the size of the search space. The number of possible snakes grows explosively with $n$. Any principled way to cut the space down, by saying "you only need to look at snakes of *this* special shape", is valuable.

This article is about one proposed cut, the **turn-minimal normal form**, and about what happened when it was examined carefully.

## Snakes as two-dimensional pictures

The key move is to see the hypercube as a product. Split the $n$ bits into two groups: the first $a$ bits, which we call the **row**, and the remaining $b = n - a$ bits, which we call the **column**. Each corner of $Q_n$ is then a pair (row, column). One step of a snake flips one bit, so it changes either the row or the column, never both. In the language of graph theory, $Q_n$ is the **box product** $Q_a \,\square\, Q_b$. You can picture it as a grid whose rows are copies of $Q_b$ and whose columns are copies of $Q_a$.

Now follow a snake and write down only its row at each moment. You get the snake's **row sequence**. Most steps leave the row alone, because they flip a column bit. Occasionally a step flips a row bit and the snake jumps to another row. Call such a step a **turn**, or **direction change**. The **turn count** is the number of turns.

Here is the picture to keep in mind. A snake crawls along inside one row for a while, which means it is wandering through a copy of the smaller hypercube $Q_b$. Then it hops to a neighbouring row and crawls there, then hops again. The stretches between hops are called **blocks**.

## The comb: the tidiest possible snake

Suppose a snake visits $r$ different rows. It needs at least $r - 1$ hops to reach all of them, since each hop brings in at most one new row. When can it get away with exactly $r - 1$? Only when it never goes back to a row it has already left. Each row is then visited in one unbroken stretch, and the row sequence looks like

$$\underbrace{A\,A\,A\,A}_{\text{row }A}\;\underbrace{B\,B\,B}_{\text{row }B}\;\underbrace{C\,C\,C\,C\,C}_{\text{row }C}\;\cdots$$

Drawn as a picture, this looks like the teeth of a comb, and the name stuck: a row sequence in which every row occupies a single contiguous block is a **comb**.

> **The Comb Theorem.** A row sequence that visits $r$ distinct rows makes at least $r - 1$ turns. It makes exactly $r - 1$ turns if and only if it is a comb.

The proof is a counting argument. Cut the sequence at each turn. A sequence with $t$ turns falls into $t + 1$ maximal blocks, and each block is a run of one row. Every visited row owns at least one block, so $t + 1 \ge r$. Equality holds exactly when each row owns *exactly* one block, and that is the definition of a comb.

So among all ways to visit a given set of rows, the comb uses the fewest direction changes, and it is the only arrangement that does. This is the formal sense of the phrase "turn-minimal".

## Why turns matter: the conjecture

Combs matter in practice because many of the best constructions of long snakes are *product constructions*. You take snakes in a smaller cube, lay them out as the teeth of a comb, and join them with short connectors. At each interface, where the snake hops from one row to the next, the construction sacrifices a little: roughly one connector cell per hop. The more turns a construction has, the more it loses.

That observation led to an attractive conjecture.

> **Turn-Minimal Normal Form Conjecture.** Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ can be transformed into a snake of length at least $L - O(n)$ that has only $O(L/n)$ direction changes.

If true, it would justify a large practical shortcut: record searches could look only at snakes with few turns and give up at most a small, explicitly bounded amount of length.

There was also a pessimistic counter-hypothesis: *direction changes are essential to long snakes*, so any product method must give up a constant fraction of length.

Both hunches turn out to be right, in a precise sense.

## The first surprise: snakes must turn

Start with the pessimistic side. A block, meaning a stretch during which the row is constant, lies entirely inside one copy of the column cube $Q_b$. The snake rule still applies inside that block. If two corners within the block were adjacent without being consecutive, they would be adjacent in $Q_n$ too, which the rule forbids. So:

> **The Block Lemma.** Every block of a snake in a product $G \,\square\, H$ is itself a snake in the factor $H$.

So no block can be longer than the longest snake in $H$. A block of a snake in $Q_n$ contains at most $S(b) + 1$ corners. A snake with $t$ turns has $t + 1$ blocks, and the snake of length $L$ has $L + 1$ corners, so

$$L + 1 \;\le\; (t + 1)\,\bigl(S(b) + 1\bigr) \;\le\; (t+1)\, 2^{b}.$$

> **Direction Changes Are Essential.** If every snake in $H$ has length at most $S$, then every snake of length $L$ in $G \,\square\, H$ makes at least $\frac{L+1}{S+1} - 1$ turns. In particular, a snake of length $L$ in $Q_{a+b}$ changes its first $a$ coordinates at least $\frac{L+1}{2^b} - 1$ times.

A long snake cannot stay inside one row; it is forced to hop. This is a lower bound on turns, and it holds for every way of choosing the rows.

There is also an exact bookkeeping identity behind all of this. Every step changes the row or the column but never both, so

$$(\text{number of row turns}) + (\text{number of column turns}) = L.$$

We call this **step accounting**. It means the row and the column always share the snake's total length between them.

## The second surprise: the conjecture is true, and costs nothing

Now the optimistic side. Can we always find a way of looking at a snake in which it turns rarely?

Look at a single snake and count how often it flips each coordinate. Call this list of $n$ numbers the snake's **flip profile**. Every step flips exactly one coordinate, so the flip profile adds up to exactly $L$. The average coordinate is therefore flipped $L/n$ times, and *some* coordinate is flipped at most $L/n$ times.

Choose that least-flipped coordinate to be the row. The row sequence changes exactly when this coordinate flips, so the snake makes at most $L/n$ turns in the split $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_{n-1}$.

To put it in standard position, relabel the coordinates so that the chosen one comes first. Permuting coordinates is a symmetry of the hypercube: it maps edges to edges and non-edges to non-edges, so it maps snakes to snakes of exactly the same length. **The snake loses no length at all.**

The same averaging works for any number $a$ of row coordinates. Over all $\binom{n}{a}$ choices of an $a$-element row set, each coordinate belongs to a fraction $a/n$ of them, so the average number of turns is $aL/n$. Some choice does at least as well as the average.

> **The Averaging Normal Form.** For every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and every $1 \le a \le n$, after a relabelling of coordinates (which preserves the length exactly), the snake's row sequence in the split $Q_a \,\square\, Q_{n-a}$ makes at most $aL/n$ turns. Combined with the lower bound,
> $$\frac{L+1}{2^{\,n-a}} - 1 \;\le\; \text{turns} \;\le\; \frac{aL}{n}.$$

For $a = 1$ this is the conjectured $O(L/n)$ bound on direction changes, with loss $0$ instead of $O(n)$.

## So what did we learn?

At first glance this looks like a triumph: the conjecture is proved, with a better constant than hoped. The honest reading is more modest, and more useful.

The conjecture is **true but cheap**. Once a "turn" is defined as a change in a chosen set of coordinates, the bound follows from averaging, and nothing about the structure of long snakes is used. Every snake, long or short, good or bad, satisfies it. A normal form that every object already satisfies does not shrink a search space.

The analysis therefore points to where the real difficulty lies. A useful normal form must say something about the **blocks**, and not only how many there are. The Block Lemma says each block is a snake of the smaller cube $Q_{n-1}$. A strong normal form would require most blocks to be *long* snakes of $Q_{n-1}$, so that the snake is built mostly from near-record pieces. That statement is not cheap, and it is now the central open question.

## What the records say

To see how real record snakes behave, we computed flip profiles of record snakes in small dimensions. The results show more structure than the averaging argument predicts.

* In $Q_5$, a longest snake (length $13$) has flip profile $(4, 3, 3, 2, 1)$. One coordinate flips **once**, so the snake is a one-turn comb in $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_4$: two snakes of $Q_4$ joined by a single hop.
* In $Q_6$, the longest snake (length $26$) found by our search has flip profile $(6, 5, 2, 5, 6, 2)$. Its least-flipped coordinate flips twice.
* In $Q_7$, a snake of length $48$ appears as a one-turn comb: one coordinate flips once, and the snake is two snakes of $Q_6$ of total length $47 = 2\cdot 26 - 5$ joined by one hop. A quick search finds a similar one-turn comb of length $47 = 25 + 1 + 21$ within seconds.

Two patterns stand out. First, the lower bound $\lceil (L+1)/(S(n-1)+1) \rceil - 1$ on the least-flipped coordinate equals $1$ in each of these cases, and the records meet it exactly for $n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 7$. The only exception is the single $26$-snake in $Q_6$, which was not chosen for this property. Second, the least-flipped coordinate is flipped at most $L/(2n)$ times in each record we examined ($13 \to 1$, $26 \to 2$, $48 \to 1$), a factor of two below what averaging guarantees.

Both patterns suggest that the best snakes really are close to combs built from very long pieces, which is the stronger normal form the analysis calls for.

## Open roads

Four conjectures come out of this work.

1. **Comb saturation.** Some longest snake in $Q_n$ has a split in which its number of turns equals the lower bound $\lceil (S(n)+1)/(S(n-a)+1)\rceil - 1$.
2. **The one-turn doubling gap.** $S(n) \ge 2S(n-1) - c$ for an absolute constant $c$, realised by one-turn combs. A one-turn comb is a pair of snakes in $Q_{n-1}$ that meet only at the hop point. This is a packing problem that SAT solvers can attack directly.
3. **Uneven flip profiles.** In every longest snake in $Q_n$ with $n \ge 5$, the least-flipped coordinate is flipped at most $L/(2n)$ times.
4. **Block-maximal normal form.** Every snake can be modified, at a cost of $O(n)$ in length, so that in some split all but $O(1)$ of its blocks have length at least $S(n-1)/2$.

The overall picture is simple to state. A snake in the hypercube can always be viewed so that it hops rarely, and this costs nothing. It can never avoid hopping entirely, since the Block Lemma forces it to. What remains open is whether the pieces between the hops can always be made long.

## Abstract

A *snake* in a graph is an induced path. The snake-in-the-box problem asks for the maximum length $S(n)$ of a snake in the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$. Many record constructions are product constructions: they view $Q_n$ as a box product $Q_a \,\square\, Q_b$ and assemble long snakes of the factor $Q_b$ into a "comb". Such constructions lose roughly one connector per change of the row coordinate. This motivates the conjecture that every snake can be normalised, at a cost of $O(n)$ in length, so that it has only $O(L/n)$ direction changes.

We study a *turn count* for snakes in box products and prove four facts. (i) **The Comb Theorem:** a row sequence that visits $r$ distinct rows has at least $r-1$ turns, with equality exactly for combs. (ii) **Step accounting:** in any box product, row turns plus column turns equals length. (iii) **Direction changes are essential:** if all snakes of $H$ have length at most $S$, then every snake of length $L$ in $G \,\square\, H$ satisfies $L+1 \le (t+1)(S+1)$, where $t$ is its turn count; in $Q_{a+b}$ this gives $L + 1 \le (t+1)2^b$ unconditionally. (iv) **The averaging normal form:** for every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and every $1 \le a \le n$, some $a$-set of row coordinates yields at most $aL/n$ turns, and a coordinate permutation moves this set into standard position at zero cost in length. The normal-form conjecture therefore holds with loss $0$ rather than $O(n)$.

We argue that this makes the conjecture *true but cheap*, and that the real content lies in a stronger, block-maximal normal form. Computations on record snakes for $n \le 7$ support this. The least-flipped coordinate of each record meets the block lower bound in every case but one, and sits a factor of two below the averaging bound. We give algorithms for the computations, numerical data, and four conjectures.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Snakes in the box

Let $Q_n$ be the graph on $\{0,1\}^n$ in which two vertices are adjacent exactly when their Hamming distance is $1$. A *snake* of length $L$ is a sequence of distinct vertices $p_0, p_1, \dots, p_L$ such that $p_i$ and $p_j$ are adjacent if and only if $|i - j| = 1$. In other words, it is a path that is an induced subgraph. The maximum length $S(n)$ is known for $n \le 7$:

$$S(1), \dots, S(7) \;=\; 1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 7,\ 13,\ 26,\ 50.$$

For $n \ge 8$ only lower bounds are known, obtained by heuristic and exhaustive computer search together with algebraic and product constructions. Snakes were first studied as error-detecting codes for analog-to-digital conversion. The search space grows super-exponentially, so restrictions that provably lose little are valuable.

### 1.2 Product constructions and turns

Splitting the coordinates of $Q_{a+b}$ into a first block of $a$ and a second block of $b$ identifies $Q_{a+b}$ with the box product $Q_a \,\square\, Q_b$. Under this identification a snake has a *row sequence*, its $Q_a$-coordinate, and a *column sequence*, its $Q_b$-coordinate. A *turn* (or direction change) is a step at which the row changes. Product constructions such as the comb place long snakes of $Q_b$ in successive rows and connect them at the turns. Each interface costs a constant number of cells, so the total loss of such a construction grows with the number of turns.

This suggests the following conjecture.

**Conjecture 0 (Turn-minimal normal form).** Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ can be transformed into a snake of length at least $L - O(n)$ whose row sequence, in a suitable product decomposition, has $O(L/n)$ direction changes.

The opposite hypothesis is that direction changes are *essential* to long snakes, so that product methods always lose a constant fraction.

### 1.3 Results

We prove the following.

* **Theorem 3.2 (Comb Theorem).** Turns $\ge$ rows $-\,1$, with equality iff comb.
* **Theorem 4.1 (Step accounting).** In any box product $G \,\square\, H$, row turns $+$ column turns $=$ length, for every walk.
* **Lemma 4.2 (Block Lemma).** Every block of constant row of a snake in $G \,\square\, H$ is a snake in $H$.
* **Theorem 4.3 (Direction changes are essential).** $L + 1 \le (t+1)(S+1)$ whenever $S$ bounds the snakes of $H$.
* **Corollary 5.3.** For snakes in $Q_{a+b}$: $L + 1 \le (t_R + 1)(S(b)+1) \le (t_R+1)2^b$.
* **Theorem 5.5 (Averaging normal form).** For every $a$ there is a split $Q_a \,\square\, Q_{n-a}$, reached by an automorphism, with $\frac{L+1}{2^{n-a}} - 1 \le t \le \frac{aL}{n}$.

Together these settle Conjecture 0 with zero loss. They also confirm the essential-turns hypothesis as a lower bound. Section 7 explains why the result is weaker than it looks, and Section 8 states sharper conjectures backed by data.

---

## 2. Definitions

Throughout, $G = (V, E_G)$ and $H = (W, E_H)$ are simple graphs. We write $x \sim_G y$ for adjacency.

**Definition 2.1 (Snake on a window).** Let $p : \mathbb{N} \to V$ and $a \le b$. We say $p$ is a *snake in $G$ on $[a, b]$* if

1. $p$ is injective on $\{a, a+1, \dots, b\}$, and
2. for all $i, j \in [a, b]$: $p_i \sim_G p_j \iff |i - j| = 1$.

A *snake of length $L$* is a snake on $[0, L]$. It has $L$ edges and $L + 1$ vertices.

**Definition 2.2 (Snake bound).** A number $S$ is a *snake bound* for $G$ if every snake in $G$ on any window $[a, b]$ satisfies $b - a \le S$. For finite $G$, $|V| - 1$ is a snake bound, since a snake visits distinct vertices. We write $S(n)$ for the least snake bound of $Q_n$, which is the snake-in-the-box number.

**Definition 2.3 (Walk).** $p$ is a *walk of length $L$* if $p_s \sim p_{s+1}$ for all $s < L$. Every snake is a walk.

**Definition 2.4 (Box product).** $G \,\square\, H$ has vertex set $V \times W$, and $(g, h) \sim (g', h')$ iff either $g \sim_G g'$ and $h = h'$, or $g = g'$ and $h \sim_H h'$.

**Definition 2.5 (Turn count).** For any sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to X$ and any $L$,
$$\tau(f, L) \;=\; \#\{\, s < L : f(s) \neq f(s+1) \,\}.$$
For a walk $p$ in $G \,\square\, H$, the *row sequence* is $s \mapsto (p_s)_1$ and the *column sequence* is $s \mapsto (p_s)_2$. The *turn count* of $p$ is $\tau$ of its row sequence.

**Definition 2.6 (Blocks; comb).** A *block* of a sequence $f$ on $[0, L]$ is a maximal interval of indices on which $f$ is constant. The sequence is a *comb* if, for each value $x$, the index set $\{s \le L : f(s) = x\}$ is an interval. Equivalently, every value occupies exactly one block.

**Definition 2.7 (Coordinate split).** For $x \in \{0,1\}^{a+b}$ let $\mathrm{split}(x) = (x|_{[1,a]},\, x|_{[a+1,a+b]}) \in \{0,1\}^a \times \{0,1\}^b$. More generally, for $R \subseteq [n]$, the *$R$-row sequence* of a snake is its restriction to the coordinates in $R$, and $t_R$ denotes its turn count.

**Definition 2.8 (Flip profile).** For a walk $p$ in $Q_n$, the *flip count* $\varphi_i$ of coordinate $i$ is the number of steps $s < L$ at which $p_s$ and $p_{s+1}$ differ in coordinate $i$. The vector $(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n)$ is the *flip profile*.

---

## 3. The Comb Theorem

**Lemma 3.1 (Block count).** A sequence $f$ on $[0, L]$ with $\tau(f, L) = t$ has exactly $t + 1$ blocks.

*Proof.* The blocks are separated exactly by the indices $s$ with $f(s) \ne f(s+1)$. Cutting $[0, L]$ at $t$ such places leaves $t+1$ intervals. $\square$

**Theorem 3.2 (Comb Theorem).** Let $f$ be a sequence on $[0, L]$ that takes $r$ distinct values. Then
$$\tau(f, L) \;\ge\; r - 1,$$
with equality if and only if $f$ is a comb.

*Proof.* Each value taken by $f$ occupies at least one block, and distinct values occupy disjoint blocks, so by Lemma 3.1 we get $t + 1 \ge r$. Equality holds iff each value occupies *exactly* one block, which is Definition 2.6. One can also argue by induction on $L$. Appending $f(L+1)$ either repeats $f(L)$, changing neither side, or changes it, adding one turn while adding at most one new value. The comb property survives the step only when the new value is either equal to $f(L)$ or genuinely new. $\square$

**Interpretation.** Among all row sequences visiting a fixed set of rows, the comb is the unique turn minimiser. "Turn-minimal" and "comb" mean the same thing.

---

## 4. Snakes in Box Products

**Theorem 4.1 (Step accounting).** Let $p$ be a walk of length $L$ in $G \,\square\, H$. Then
$$\tau\bigl(s \mapsto (p_s)_1, L\bigr) + \tau\bigl(s \mapsto (p_s)_2, L\bigr) \;=\; L.$$

*Proof.* By induction on $L$. The case $L = 0$ is trivial. For the inductive step, the edge $p_L \sim p_{L+1}$ is, by Definition 2.4, either a $G$-edge with equal second coordinates or an $H$-edge with equal first coordinates. In the first case the row changes, since adjacent vertices are distinct, and the column does not. In the second case the reverse holds. Exactly one of the two counts increases by one. $\square$

**Lemma 4.2 (Block Lemma).** Let $p$ be a snake in $G \,\square\, H$ on $[a, b]$, and suppose the row $(p_s)_1$ is constant on $[i, j] \subseteq [a, b]$. Then the column sequence $s \mapsto (p_s)_2$ is a snake in $H$ on $[i, j]$.

*Proof.* Injectivity: if $(p_s)_2 = (p_{s'})_2$ for $s, s' \in [i,j]$, then $p_s = p_{s'}$ because the rows also agree, so $s = s'$. Induced adjacency: for vertices with equal first coordinate, $(g, h) \sim (g, h')$ iff $h \sim_H h'$, since the $G$-edge alternative needs $g \sim_G g$, which is impossible in a simple graph. So $(p_s)_2 \sim_H (p_{s'})_2 \iff p_s \sim p_{s'} \iff |s - s'| = 1$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.3 (Direction changes are essential).** Suppose $S$ is a snake bound for $H$. If $p$ is a snake of length $L$ in $G \,\square\, H$ with turn count $t$, then
$$L + 1 \;\le\; (t + 1)(S + 1).$$
Equivalently, $t \ge \frac{L+1}{S+1} - 1$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.1 the row sequence has $t + 1$ blocks, which partition the $L + 1$ indices. By Lemma 4.2 each block $[i, j]$ carries a snake of $H$ on $[i,j]$, so $j - i \le S$ and the block has at most $S + 1$ indices. Summing gives the bound. Formally one proceeds by induction on $L$, tracking the length of the final block. $\square$

**Remark 4.4.** Theorem 4.3 is the formal version of the slogan "direction changes are essential". A snake much longer than $S$ cannot stay in one row, and the number of rows it must pass through, counted with multiplicity, grows linearly in $L/S$.

---

## 5. Hypercubes

**Lemma 5.1 (Hamming distance splits).** For $x, y \in \{0,1\}^{a+b}$,
$$d_H(x, y) \;=\; d_H\bigl(x|_{[1,a]}, y|_{[1,a]}\bigr) + d_H\bigl(x|_{[a+1,a+b]}, y|_{[a+1,a+b]}\bigr).$$

*Proof.* The set of differing coordinates is the disjoint union of the differing coordinates in each block. $\square$

**Theorem 5.2 (The hypercube is a box product).** The map $\mathrm{split}$ is a bijection $\{0,1\}^{a+b} \to \{0,1\}^a \times \{0,1\}^b$, and for all $x, y$,
$$x \sim_{Q_{a+b}} y \iff \mathrm{split}(x) \sim_{Q_a \square Q_b} \mathrm{split}(y).$$

*Proof.* Injectivity is clear, since a vector is determined by its two halves. By Lemma 5.1, $d_H(x,y) = 1$ iff one half has distance $1$ and the other has distance $0$, that is, the halves are equal. This is exactly Definition 2.4. $\square$

**Transfer principle.** If $f : V \to W$ is injective and preserves and reflects adjacency, then $f \circ p$ is a snake in the target whenever $p$ is a snake in the source, on the same window. This follows directly from Definition 2.1. In particular, snakes in $Q_{a+b}$ correspond to snakes in $Q_a \,\square\, Q_b$.

**Corollary 5.3 (Turn bounds in $Q_n$).** Let $p$ be a snake of length $L$ in $Q_{a+b}$, and let $t$ and $t'$ be the numbers of steps flipping one of the first $a$, respectively last $b$, coordinates. Then:

1. $t + t' = L$;
2. if $S$ is a snake bound for $Q_b$, then $L + 1 \le (t+1)(S+1)$;
3. unconditionally, $L + 1 \le (t + 1)\, 2^b$.

*Proof.* Transfer $p$ along $\mathrm{split}$ using Theorem 5.2. Then (1) is Theorem 4.1, and (2) is Theorem 4.3. For (3), apply (2) with the trivial snake bound $|V(Q_b)| - 1 = 2^b - 1$. $\square$

**Lemma 5.4 (Turns are flips).** For any $R \subseteq [n]$, the $R$-row sequence of a walk in $Q_n$ changes at step $s$ iff the coordinate flipped at step $s$ lies in $R$. Hence
$$t_R = \sum_{i \in R} \varphi_i, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i = L.$$

*Proof.* Each step flips exactly one coordinate. $\square$

**Theorem 5.5 (Averaging normal form).** Let $p$ be a snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and $1 \le a \le n$. There is an $a$-set $R \subseteq [n]$ with
$$\frac{L+1}{2^{\,n-a}} - 1 \;\le\; t_R \;\le\; \frac{aL}{n}.$$
Moreover, there is a coordinate permutation $\sigma$, which is an automorphism of $Q_n$, such that $\sigma \circ p$ is a snake of the *same* length $L$ whose row sequence in the standard split $Q_a \,\square\, Q_{n-a}$ has exactly $t_R$ turns.

*Proof.* By Lemma 5.4,
$$\sum_{|R| = a} t_R \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i \cdot \#\{R \ni i\} \;=\; \binom{n-1}{a-1} L,$$
so the average of $t_R$ over the $\binom{n}{a}$ sets is $\frac{a}{n}L$, and some $R$ is at most average. The minimiser is simply the set of the $a$ least-flipped coordinates. The lower bound is Corollary 5.3(3), applied after the permutation $\sigma$ that sends $R$ to $\{1, \dots, a\}$. Coordinate permutations preserve Hamming distance, so by the transfer principle $\sigma \circ p$ is a snake of length $L$. $\square$

**Corollary 5.6 (Conjecture 0 with zero loss).** Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ is, after an automorphism of $Q_n$, a snake of the same length whose row sequence in $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_{n-1}$ has at most $L/n$ direction changes. In particular, the least-flipped coordinate of any snake satisfies
$$\frac{L+1}{S(n-1)+1} - 1 \;\le\; \min_i \varphi_i \;\le\; \frac{L}{n}.$$

---

## 6. Algorithms

**Algorithm A (Turn-minimal split).** *Input:* the transition sequence $c_1, \dots, c_L \in [n]$ of a snake, where $c_s$ is the coordinate flipped at step $s$, and an integer $a$. *Output:* an $a$-set $R$ minimising $t_R$, and the relabelling $\sigma$.

1. Compute the flip profile $\varphi_i = \#\{s : c_s = i\}$ in $O(L + n)$ time.
2. Sort the coordinates by $\varphi_i$ and take the $a$ smallest as $R$, in $O(n \log n)$ time.
3. Let $\sigma$ send $R$ to $\{1, \dots, a\}$ in order and the complement to $\{a+1, \dots, n\}$; output $\sigma(c_1), \dots, \sigma(c_L)$.

By Lemma 5.4 and Theorem 5.5 the output has exactly $t_R \le aL/n$ turns and the same length.

**Algorithm B (Record search with symmetry breaking).** Depth-first search over transition sequences starting at $0^n$. Keep, for every vertex $w$, the number $\mathrm{adj}(w)$ of path vertices adjacent to $w$. A vertex $w$ adjacent to the tail may be appended iff $w$ is unused and $\mathrm{adj}(w) = 1$, meaning the tail is its only path neighbour. Updates cost $O(n)$ per step. Coordinates are introduced in increasing order: the first flip of coordinate $i$ comes after the first flip of $i-1$. This removes the $n!$ coordinate-permutation symmetry. With this pruning, records for $n \le 6$ are found in under a second.

**Algorithm C (One-turn comb).** Given a snake $A$ in $Q_{n-1}$ ending at $u$, search for a snake $B$ in $Q_{n-1}$ starting at $u$ whose other vertices avoid the vertex set of $A$. Then $A$, followed by a flip of coordinate $n$, followed by $B$ is a snake in $Q_n$ of length $|A| + 1 + |B|$, whose row sequence in $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_{n-1}$ is a comb with one turn. *Correctness:* vertices $(0, x)$ and $(1, y)$ are adjacent iff $x = y$, so the only cross-layer adjacency is at the hop. Within each layer, the snake property of $A$ and of $B$ handles everything else.

---

## 7. Discussion: true but cheap

Corollary 5.6 proves Conjecture 0 with a loss of $0$ instead of $O(n)$. The proof should still make one wary. It uses no property of long snakes: every walk in $Q_n$ that changes one coordinate per step satisfies the averaging bound. A normal form satisfied by every snake does not reduce a search space at all.

The two sides of Theorem 5.5 explain the situation:

* the **upper bound** $t \le aL/n$ is free, because it comes from averaging;
* the **lower bound** $t \ge (L+1)/(S(n-a)+1) - 1$ is forced, because it comes from the Block Lemma.

For long snakes the gap between them is large. When $a = 1$ and $L \approx S(n) \approx 2S(n-1)$, the lower bound is about $1$ while the upper bound is about $L/n$. A meaningful normal form should push a snake towards the *lower* end. That is equivalent to asking that the blocks, which are snakes of $Q_{n-a}$ by the Block Lemma, be *long*. The Comb Theorem turns turn-minimality into a statement about block lengths, and that is where the difficulty lies.

The essential-turns hypothesis is confirmed in the weak sense of Theorem 4.3. Whether product methods must lose a constant *fraction* of length is a different question. The data in Section 8 suggest that for $a = 1$ they lose only an additive constant per doubling.

---

## 8. Numerical evidence

Using Algorithms A–C we computed flip profiles of record snakes.

| $n$ | $L$ | flip profile | $\min\varphi$ | block lower bound $\lceil\frac{L+1}{S(n-1)+1}\rceil - 1$ | $\lfloor L/n \rfloor$ | $L/(2n)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 2 | $(1,1)$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 4 | $(2,1,1)$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0.67 |
| 4 | 7 | $(3,2,1,1)$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0.88 |
| 5 | 13 | $(4,3,3,2,1)$ | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1.3 |
| 6 | 26 | $(6,5,2,5,6,2)$ | 2 | 1 | 4 | 2.17 |
| 7 | 48 | one-turn comb | 1 | 1 | 6 | 3.43 |

The $n = 7$ snake of length $48$ is a one-turn comb in $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_6$, made of two snakes of $Q_6$ of total length $47 = 2 \cdot 26 - 5$. A short run of Algorithm C, starting from the $26$-snake above, gives a one-turn comb of length $47 = 25 + 1 + 21$ in $Q_7$ within seconds, with flip profile $(9,10,5,8,11,3,1)$.

**Observations.**

1. For $a = 1$ the block lower bound is met with equality for $n = 2,3,4,5,7$. The only exception is the single $26$-snake of $Q_6$, which was not optimised for this property.
2. In every record with $n \ge 5$ the least-flipped coordinate satisfies $\min\varphi \le L/(2n)$: $13 \to 1$, $26 \to 2$, $48 \to 1$. This is a factor of two below the averaging bound.
3. Step accounting (Theorem 4.1) and the Block Lemma were checked directly on every split with $a \in \{1, 2\}$ for $n = 5, 6$.

---

## 9. Future directions

**Conjecture 1 (Comb saturation).** For every $n \ge 3$ and some $a \ge 1$, at least one longest snake in $Q_n$ has a split $Q_a \,\square\, Q_{n-a}$ whose turn count equals the lower bound $\lceil (S(n)+1)/(S(n-a)+1) \rceil - 1$. For $a = 1$ this holds in the data at $n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 7$. Flip-profile certificates make it a finite check for each $n$.

**Conjecture 2 (One-turn doubling gap).** $S(n) \ge 2S(n-1) - c$ for an absolute constant $c$, realised by one-turn combs in $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_{n-1}$. A one-turn comb is a pair of snakes in $Q_{n-1}$ that share only the hop vertex. This is a packing problem that SAT solvers can attack directly.

**Conjecture 3 (Uneven flip profile).** For every longest snake in $Q_n$ with $n \ge 5$, the least-flipped coordinate is flipped at most $L/(2n)$ times.

**Conjecture 4 (Block-maximal normal form).** Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ can be transformed into one of length $\ge L - O(n)$ such that, in some split $Q_1 \,\square\, Q_{n-1}$, every block except $O(1)$ of them has length $\ge S(n-1)/2$. By the Comb Theorem this is the natural strengthening of turn-minimality to block lengths. If it holds, record search reduces to searching for near-record snakes of $Q_{n-1}$ that can be packed together.

---

## 10. Conclusion

We introduced a turn count for snakes in box products and proved four things. Combs are exactly the turn-minimal row sequences. Row and column turns always add up to the length. Every block is a snake of the column factor, so long snakes are forced to turn. And averaging over coordinate choices gives, at zero cost, a split with at most $aL/n$ turns. The turn-minimal normal-form conjecture is therefore true, but its proof shows that turn counts alone do not capture the structure of record snakes. The data point to a sharper statement about block lengths, formulated here as four conjectures.

\begin{abstract}
A \emph{snake} in a graph is an induced path. The snake-in-the-box problem asks for the
maximum length $S(n)$ of a snake in the $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$. Many record
constructions are product constructions: they view $Q_n$ as a box product $Q_a\bx Q_b$
and assemble long snakes of the factor $Q_b$ into a ``comb''. Such constructions lose
roughly one connector per change of the row coordinate. This motivates the conjecture that
every snake can be normalised, at a cost of $O(n)$ in length, so that it has only $O(L/n)$
direction changes.

We study a turn count for snakes in box products and prove four facts.
(i)~\emph{The Comb Theorem:} a row sequence that visits $r$ distinct rows has at least
$r-1$ turns, with equality exactly for combs.
(ii)~\emph{Step accounting:} in any box product, row turns plus column turns equals length.
(iii)~\emph{Direction changes are essential:} if all snakes of $H$ have length at most $S$,
then every snake of length $L$ in $G\bx H$ satisfies $L+1\le(t+1)(S+1)$, where $t$ is its
turn count; in $Q_{a+b}$ this gives $L+1\le(t+1)2^b$ unconditionally.
(iv)~\emph{The averaging normal form:} for every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and every
$1\le a\le n$, some $a$-set of row coordinates yields at most $aL/n$ turns, and a coordinate
permutation moves this set into standard position at zero cost in length. The normal-form
conjecture therefore holds with loss $0$ rather than $O(n)$.

We argue that this makes the conjecture \emph{true but cheap}, and that the real content
lies in a stronger, block-maximal normal form. Computations on record snakes for $n\le 7$
support this. The least-flipped coordinate of each record meets the block lower bound in
every case but one, and sits a factor of two below the averaging bound. We give algorithms
for the computations, numerical data, and four conjectures.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Snakes in the box}
Let $Q_n$ be the graph on $\{0,1\}^n$ in which two vertices are adjacent exactly when their
Hamming distance is $1$. A \emph{snake} of length $L$ is a sequence of distinct vertices
$p_0,\dots,p_L$ such that $p_i$ and $p_j$ are adjacent if and only if $|i-j|=1$. In other
words, it is a path that is an induced subgraph. The maximum length $S(n)$ is known for
$n\le 7$:
\[
S(1),\dots,S(7) \;=\; 1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 7,\ 13,\ 26,\ 50.
\]
For $n\ge 8$ only lower bounds are known, obtained by heuristic and exhaustive computer
search together with algebraic and product constructions. Snakes were first studied as
error-detecting codes for analog-to-digital conversion. The search space grows
super-exponentially, so restrictions that provably lose little are valuable.

\subsection{Product constructions and turns}
Splitting the coordinates of $Q_{a+b}$ into a first block of $a$ and a second block of $b$
identifies $Q_{a+b}$ with $Q_a\bx Q_b$. Under this identification a snake has a \emph{row
sequence}, its $Q_a$-coordinate, and a \emph{column sequence}, its $Q_b$-coordinate. A
\emph{turn} (or direction change) is a step at which the row changes. Product constructions
such as the comb place long snakes of $Q_b$ in successive rows and connect them at the
turns. Each interface costs a constant number of cells, so the total loss of such a
construction grows with the number of turns.

\begin{conjecture}[Turn-minimal normal form]\label{conj:0}
Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ can be transformed into a snake of length at least
$L-O(n)$ whose row sequence, in a suitable product decomposition, has $O(L/n)$ direction
changes.
\end{conjecture}

The opposite hypothesis is that direction changes are \emph{essential} to long snakes, so
that product methods always lose a constant fraction.

\subsection{Results}
We prove the Comb Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:comb}), step accounting
(Theorem~\ref{thm:step}), the Block Lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:block}), the essential-turns
bound (Theorem~\ref{thm:essential}), its hypercube form (Corollary~\ref{cor:cube}), and the
averaging normal form (Theorem~\ref{thm:avg}). Together these settle
Conjecture~\ref{conj:0} with zero loss. They also confirm the essential-turns hypothesis as
a lower bound. Section~\ref{sec:disc} explains why the result is weaker than it looks, and
Section~\ref{sec:future} states sharper conjectures backed by data.

\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $G=(V,E_G)$ and $H=(W,E_H)$ are simple graphs. We write $x\sim_G y$ for
adjacency.

\begin{definition}[Snake on a window]
Let $p:\N\to V$ and $a\le b$. We say $p$ is a \emph{snake in $G$ on $[a,b]$} if (1)~$p$ is
injective on $\{a,\dots,b\}$, and (2)~for all $i,j\in[a,b]$, $p_i\sim_G p_j$ if and only if
$|i-j|=1$. A \emph{snake of length $L$} is a snake on $[0,L]$. It has $L$ edges and $L+1$
vertices.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Snake bound]
A number $S$ is a \emph{snake bound} for $G$ if every snake in $G$ on any window $[a,b]$
satisfies $b-a\le S$. For finite $G$, $|V|-1$ is a snake bound. We write $S(n)$ for the
least snake bound of $Q_n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Walk]
$p$ is a \emph{walk of length $L$} if $p_s\sim p_{s+1}$ for all $s<L$. Every snake is a
walk.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Box product]
$G\bx H$ has vertex set $V\times W$, and $(g,h)\sim(g',h')$ if and only if either
$g\sim_G g'$ and $h=h'$, or $g=g'$ and $h\sim_H h'$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Turn count]
For a sequence $f:\N\to X$ and $L\in\N$, let
$\tau(f,L)=\#\{s<L: f(s)\neq f(s+1)\}$. For a walk $p$ in $G\bx H$, the \emph{row sequence}
is $s\mapsto(p_s)_1$ and the \emph{column sequence} is $s\mapsto(p_s)_2$. The \emph{turn
count} of $p$ is $\tau$ of its row sequence.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Blocks; comb]
A \emph{block} of $f$ on $[0,L]$ is a maximal interval of indices on which $f$ is constant.
The sequence is a \emph{comb} if, for each value $x$, the set $\{s\le L: f(s)=x\}$ is an
interval. Equivalently, every value occupies exactly one block.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Coordinate split; flip profile]
For $x\in\{0,1\}^{a+b}$ let $\mathrm{split}(x)=(x|_{[1,a]},x|_{[a+1,a+b]})$. For
$R\subseteq[n]$, the \emph{$R$-row sequence} of a walk in $Q_n$ is its restriction to the
coordinates in $R$, and $t_R$ is its turn count. The \emph{flip count} $\varphi_i$ of
coordinate $i$ is the number of steps at which coordinate $i$ changes, and
$(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n)$ is the \emph{flip profile}.
\end{definition}

\section{The Comb Theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Block count]\label{lem:blockcount}
A sequence $f$ on $[0,L]$ with $\tau(f,L)=t$ has exactly $t+1$ blocks.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The blocks are separated exactly by the indices $s$ with $f(s)\neq f(s+1)$. Cutting
$[0,L]$ at $t$ such places leaves $t+1$ intervals.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Comb Theorem]\label{thm:comb}
Let $f$ be a sequence on $[0,L]$ that takes $r$ distinct values. Then $\tau(f,L)\ge r-1$,
with equality if and only if $f$ is a comb.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Each value occupies at least one block, and distinct values occupy disjoint blocks, so by
Lemma~\ref{lem:blockcount} we get $t+1\ge r$. Equality holds if and only if each value
occupies exactly one block, which is the definition of a comb. Alternatively, argue by
induction on $L$. Appending $f(L+1)$ either repeats $f(L)$ or adds one turn and at most one
new value. The comb property survives the step only when the new value equals $f(L)$ or is
genuinely new.
\end{proof}

Among all row sequences visiting a fixed set of rows, the comb is the unique turn
minimiser.

\section{Snakes in box products}

\begin{theorem}[Step accounting]\label{thm:step}
For every walk $p$ of length $L$ in $G\bx H$,
\[
\tau\bigl(s\mapsto(p_s)_1,L\bigr)+\tau\bigl(s\mapsto(p_s)_2,L\bigr)=L.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $L$. The edge $p_L\sim p_{L+1}$ is either a $G$-edge with equal second
coordinates or an $H$-edge with equal first coordinates. In the first case only the row
changes, since adjacent vertices are distinct, and in the second case only the column
changes. Exactly one count increases by one.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Block Lemma]\label{lem:block}
Let $p$ be a snake in $G\bx H$ on $[a,b]$ whose row is constant on $[i,j]\subseteq[a,b]$.
Then the column sequence is a snake in $H$ on $[i,j]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If two columns agree on $[i,j]$, then the vertices agree because the rows agree, so the
indices agree. For vertices with equal first coordinate, $(g,h)\sim(g,h')$ if and only if
$h\sim_H h'$, since $g\sim_G g$ is impossible. Hence the induced-adjacency condition
transfers from $p$ to its column sequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Direction changes are essential]\label{thm:essential}
If $S$ is a snake bound for $H$ and $p$ is a snake of length $L$ in $G\bx H$ with turn count
$t$, then
\[
L+1\le(t+1)(S+1),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad t\ge\frac{L+1}{S+1}-1.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The row sequence has $t+1$ blocks (Lemma~\ref{lem:blockcount}), which partition the $L+1$
indices. Each block carries a snake of $H$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:block}), so it contains at most
$S+1$ indices.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
A snake much longer than $S$ cannot stay in one row. The number of rows it passes through,
counted with multiplicity, grows linearly in $L/S$.
\end{remark}

\section{Hypercubes}

\begin{lemma}[Hamming distance splits]\label{lem:ham}
For $x,y\in\{0,1\}^{a+b}$, $d_H(x,y)=d_H(x|_{[1,a]},y|_{[1,a]})+d_H(x|_{[a+1,a+b]},y|_{[a+1,a+b]})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The differing coordinates split disjointly between the two blocks.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The hypercube is a box product]\label{thm:split}
$\mathrm{split}$ is a bijection, and $x\sim_{Q_{a+b}}y$ if and only if
$\mathrm{split}(x)\sim_{Q_a\bx Q_b}\mathrm{split}(y)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:ham}, $d_H(x,y)=1$ if and only if one half has distance $1$ and the other
has distance $0$.
\end{proof}

\emph{Transfer principle.} If $f:V\to W$ is injective and preserves and reflects adjacency,
then $f\circ p$ is a snake whenever $p$ is, on the same window.

\begin{corollary}[Turn bounds in $Q_n$]\label{cor:cube}
Let $p$ be a snake of length $L$ in $Q_{a+b}$, and let $t$ and $t'$ be the numbers of steps
flipping one of the first $a$, respectively last $b$, coordinates. Then (1)~$t+t'=L$;
(2)~if $S$ is a snake bound for $Q_b$, then $L+1\le(t+1)(S+1)$; (3)~unconditionally,
$L+1\le(t+1)2^b$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Transfer along $\mathrm{split}$ and apply Theorems~\ref{thm:step} and~\ref{thm:essential}.
For (3), use the trivial snake bound $2^b-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Turns are flips]\label{lem:flips}
For $R\subseteq[n]$, $t_R=\sum_{i\in R}\varphi_i$, and $\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi_i=L$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each step flips exactly one coordinate, and the $R$-row changes exactly when that
coordinate lies in $R$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Averaging normal form]\label{thm:avg}
Let $p$ be a snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and $1\le a\le n$. There is an $a$-set
$R\subseteq[n]$ with
\[
\frac{L+1}{2^{n-a}}-1\;\le\;t_R\;\le\;\frac{aL}{n},
\]
and a coordinate permutation $\sigma$, which is an automorphism of $Q_n$, such that
$\sigma\circ p$ is a snake of the same length $L$ whose row sequence in the standard split
$Q_a\bx Q_{n-a}$ has exactly $t_R$ turns.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:flips},
$\sum_{|R|=a}t_R=\sum_i\varphi_i\cdot\#\{R\ni i\}=\binom{n-1}{a-1}L$, so the mean of $t_R$
over all $\binom{n}{a}$ choices is $aL/n$. The set of the $a$ least-flipped coordinates
attains the minimum. Coordinate permutations preserve Hamming distance, so
$\sigma\circ p$ is a snake of length $L$. The lower bound is
Corollary~\ref{cor:cube}(3).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Conjecture~\ref{conj:0} with zero loss]\label{cor:zero}
Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ is, after an automorphism, a snake of the same length
whose row sequence in $Q_1\bx Q_{n-1}$ has at most $L/n$ direction changes. Moreover
\[
\frac{L+1}{S(n-1)+1}-1\;\le\;\min_i\varphi_i\;\le\;\frac{L}{n}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithm}[Turn-minimal split]
Input: a transition sequence $c_1,\dots,c_L\in[n]$ and $a$.
(1)~Compute $\varphi_i=\#\{s:c_s=i\}$ in $O(L+n)$ time.
(2)~Take $R$ to be the $a$ coordinates with the smallest $\varphi_i$, in $O(n\log n)$ time.
(3)~Let $\sigma$ send $R$ to $\{1,\dots,a\}$ and output $\sigma(c_1),\dots,\sigma(c_L)$.
The output has the same length and $t_R\le aL/n$ turns.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Record search with symmetry breaking]
Depth-first search from $0^n$, keeping for each vertex $w$ the number $\mathrm{adj}(w)$ of
path vertices adjacent to it. A neighbour $w$ of the tail may be appended if and only if it
is unused and $\mathrm{adj}(w)=1$. Coordinates are introduced in increasing order, which
removes the $n!$ permutation symmetry. Records for $n\le 6$ are found in under a second.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[One-turn comb]
Given a snake $A$ in $Q_{n-1}$ ending at $u$, search for a snake $B$ in $Q_{n-1}$ from $u$
whose other vertices avoid $A$. Then $A$, a flip of coordinate $n$, and $B$ together form a
snake of length $|A|+1+|B|$ in $Q_n$, whose row sequence in $Q_1\bx Q_{n-1}$ is a comb with
one turn. This is correct because $(0,x)\sim(1,y)$ if and only if $x=y$.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Discussion: true but cheap}\label{sec:disc}

Corollary~\ref{cor:zero} proves Conjecture~\ref{conj:0} with loss $0$ instead of $O(n)$.
The proof uses no property of long snakes: every walk in $Q_n$ satisfies the averaging
bound. A normal form satisfied by every snake does not shrink a search space. The upper
bound $t\le aL/n$ is free, because it comes from averaging. The lower bound
$t\ge(L+1)/(S(n-a)+1)-1$ is forced, because it comes from the Block Lemma. For long snakes
with $a=1$ the lower bound is about $1$ while the upper bound is about $L/n$. A meaningful
normal form must push snakes towards the lower end. By the Comb Theorem, this means asking
for \emph{long blocks}.

\section{Numerical evidence}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccccc}
\toprule
$n$ & $L$ & flip profile & $\min\varphi$ & $\lceil\frac{L+1}{S(n-1)+1}\rceil-1$ & $\lfloor L/n\rfloor$\\
\midrule
2 & 2 & $(1,1)$ & 1 & 1 & 1\\
3 & 4 & $(2,1,1)$ & 1 & 1 & 1\\
4 & 7 & $(3,2,1,1)$ & 1 & 1 & 1\\
5 & 13 & $(4,3,3,2,1)$ & 1 & 1 & 2\\
6 & 26 & $(6,5,2,5,6,2)$ & 2 & 1 & 4\\
7 & 48 & one-turn comb & 1 & 1 & 6\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The $n=7$ snake of length $48$ is a one-turn comb in $Q_1\bx Q_6$, made of two snakes of
$Q_6$ of total length $47=2\cdot26-5$. A short run of the one-turn comb search, starting
from the $26$-snake above, gives a one-turn comb of length $47=25+1+21$ with flip profile
$(9,10,5,8,11,3,1)$. For $a=1$ the block lower bound is met with equality for
$n=2,3,4,5,7$. The only exception is the single $26$-snake of $Q_6$, which was not
optimised for this property. In every record with $n\ge5$, $\min\varphi\le L/(2n)$.

\section{Future directions}\label{sec:future}

\begin{conjecture}[Comb saturation]
For every $n\ge 3$ and some $a\ge1$, at least one longest snake in $Q_n$ has a split
$Q_a\bx Q_{n-a}$ whose turn count equals $\lceil (S(n)+1)/(S(n-a)+1)\rceil-1$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[One-turn doubling gap]
$S(n)\ge 2S(n-1)-c$ for an absolute constant $c$, realised by one-turn combs in
$Q_1\bx Q_{n-1}$.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Uneven flip profile]
For every longest snake in $Q_n$ with $n\ge5$, the least-flipped coordinate is flipped at
most $L/(2n)$ times.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Block-maximal normal form]
Every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ can be transformed into one of length $\ge L-O(n)$ such
that, in some split $Q_1\bx Q_{n-1}$, every block except $O(1)$ of them has length
$\ge S(n-1)/2$.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}
Combs are exactly the turn-minimal row sequences. Row and column turns always add up to the
length. Every block is a snake of the column factor, so long snakes are forced to turn. And
averaging over coordinate choices gives, at zero cost, a split with at most $aL/n$ turns.
The turn-minimal normal-form conjecture is therefore true, but its proof shows that turn
counts alone do not capture the structure of record snakes. The data point to a sharper
statement about block lengths.

\end{document}

     gives the unconditional bound L + 1 <= (turns + 1) * 2^b.

import math
import random
import sys
import time
from typing import Callable, Dict, Hashable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Hypercube snakes
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def vertices_from_transitions(trans: Sequence[int], start: int = 0) -> List[int]:
    """Vertex sequence p_0, ..., p_L of the walk with the given transition sequence."""
    verts = [start]
    for c in trans:
        verts.append(verts[-1] ^ (1 << c))
    return verts


def hamming(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return bin(x ^ y).count("1")


def is_snake(verts: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """Induced path: distinct vertices, adjacent exactly when consecutive."""
    L = len(verts) - 1
    if len(set(verts)) != len(verts):
        return False
    for i in range(L + 1):
        for j in range(i + 1, L + 1):
            if (hamming(verts[i], verts[j]) == 1) != (j == i + 1):
                return False
    return True


def longest_snake(n: int, target: Optional[int] = None,
                  time_limit: float = 60.0) -> List[int]:
    """Depth-first search for a long snake in Q_n.

    Symmetry breaking: start at vertex 0 and introduce coordinates in increasing
    order (the first use of coordinate i happens after the first use of i-1).
    A vertex may be appended iff it is unused and adjacent to exactly one path
    vertex, namely the current tail.  Returns the transition sequence of the
    longest snake found (stops early once `target` is reached).
    """
    N = 1 << n
    adj_count = [0] * N
    on_path = [False] * N
    on_path[0] = True
    for i in range(n):
        adj_count[1 << i] += 1
    path: List[int] = [0]
    trans: List[int] = []
    best: List[int] = []
    deadline = time.time() + time_limit

    def rec(max_coord: int) -> bool:
        nonlocal best
        if len(trans) > len(best):
            best = list(trans)
        if target is not None and len(best) >= target:
            return True
        if time.time() > deadline:
            return True
        v = path[-1]
        for i in range(min(n, max_coord + 1)):
            w = v ^ (1 << i)
            if on_path[w] or adj_count[w] != 1:
                continue
            path.append(w); trans.append(i); on_path[w] = True
            for j in range(n):
                adj_count[w ^ (1 << j)] += 1
            if rec(max(max_coord, i + 1)):
                return True
            for j in range(n):
                adj_count[w ^ (1 << j)] -= 1
            path.pop(); trans.pop(); on_path[w] = False
        return False

    rec(0)
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Turn counts and combs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def turn_count(seq: Sequence[Hashable]) -> int:
    """Number of indices s with seq[s] != seq[s+1]."""
    return sum(1 for s in range(len(seq) - 1) if seq[s] != seq[s + 1])


def is_comb(seq: Sequence[Hashable]) -> bool:
    """Every value occupies one contiguous block of indices."""
    seen = set()
    for s, x in enumerate(seq):
        if s > 0 and x != seq[s - 1] and x in seen:
            return False
        seen.add(x)
    return True


def blocks(seq: Sequence[Hashable]) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Maximal constant blocks as inclusive index intervals [start, end]."""
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    start = 0
    for s in range(1, len(seq) + 1):
        if s == len(seq) or seq[s] != seq[start]:
            out.append((start, s - 1))
            start = s
    return out


def check_comb_theorem(alphabet: int = 3, max_len: int = 8) -> int:
    """Exhaustively check: turns >= r - 1, with equality iff comb."""
    checked = 0
    for length in range(1, max_len + 1):
        for seq in itertools.product(range(alphabet), repeat=length):
            r = len(set(seq))
            t = turn_count(seq)
            assert t >= r - 1
            assert (t == r - 1) == is_comb(seq)
            checked += 1
    return checked


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Coordinate splits Q_{a+b} = Q_a x Q_b
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def project(v: int, coords: Sequence[int]) -> Tuple[int, ...]:
    """Restriction of the vertex v to the coordinates in `coords`."""
    return tuple((v >> c) & 1 for c in coords)


def row_col_sequences(verts: Sequence[int], row_coords: Sequence[int],

    prof = flip_profile(trans, n)
    best = tuple(sorted(sorted(range(n), key=lambda c: (prof[c], c))[:a]))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def one_turn_comb(A: Sequence[int], n_minus_1: int, time_limit: float = 20.0) -> List[int]:
    """Given a snake A in Q_{n-1} (transition list from 0), search a second snake B in
    Q_{n-1} starting at A's endpoint and avoiding A's other vertices.  The walk
    A, (flip new coordinate), B is then a snake in Q_n with exactly one turn in the
    new coordinate.  Returns the transitions of B."""
    m = n_minus_1
    verts = vertices_from_transitions(A)
    forbidden = set(verts[:-1])
    u = verts[-1]
    best: List[int] = []
    deadline = time.time() + time_limit

    def ok(w: int, on: set, v: int) -> bool:
        if w in forbidden or w in on:
            return False
        return not any((w ^ (1 << j)) in on and (w ^ (1 << j)) != v for j in range(m))

    def rec(path: List[int], on: set, tr: List[int]) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        if len(tr) > len(best):
            best = list(tr)
        if time.time() > deadline:
            return
        v = path[-1]
        for i in range(m):
            w = v ^ (1 << i)
            if ok(w, on, v):
                path.append(w); on.add(w); tr.append(i)
                rec(path, on, tr)
                path.pop(); on.discard(w); tr.pop()

    rec([u], {u}, [])
    return best


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 78)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 78)


def main() -> None:
    random.seed(2026)

    banner("1. The Comb Theorem (exhaustive check on short sequences)")
    k = check_comb_theorem(3, 8)
    print(f"checked {k} sequences over a 3-letter alphabet: "
          f"turns >= rows - 1, with equality exactly for combs.")
    ex_comb = list("AAABBCCCC")
    ex_back = list("AABBAACCC")
    for ex in (ex_comb, ex_back):
        print(f"  {''.join(ex)}: rows={len(set(ex))}, turns={turn_count(ex)}, comb={is_comb(ex)}")

    banner("2. Record snakes for n <= 6 (depth-first search)")
    S: Dict[int, int] = {0: 0}
    records: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    known = {1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 4, 4: 7, 5: 13, 6: 26}
    for n in range(1, 7):
        t0 = time.time()
        tr = longest_snake(n, target=known[n], time_limit=60)
        verts = vertices_from_transitions(tr)
        assert is_snake(verts)
        S[n] = len(tr)
        records[n] = tr
        print(f"  n={n}: length {len(tr):2d} (known maximum {known[n]:2d})  "
              f"[{time.time() - t0:.2f}s]  transitions={tr}")

    banner("3. Step accounting and the turn lower bound in Q_n = Q_a x Q_b")
    for n in (5, 6):
        tr = records[n]
        verts = vertices_from_transitions(tr)
        L = len(tr)
        for a in (1, 2):
            R = list(range(a))
            rows, cols = row_col_sequences(verts, R, n)
            rt, ct = turn_count(rows), turn_count(cols)
            b = n - a
            assert rt + ct == L
            # Block lemma: every row block is a snake of the column factor
            for (s, e) in blocks(rows):
                block_cols = [int("".join(map(str, c)) or "0", 2) for c in cols[s:e + 1]]
                assert is_snake(block_cols)
            assert L + 1 <= (rt + 1) * (S[b] + 1) <= (rt + 1) * 2 ** b
            print(f"  n={n}, L={L}, rows=first {a} coord(s): row turns={rt}, col turns={ct}, "
                  f"sum={rt + ct};  L+1={L + 1} <= (rt+1)(S({b})+1)={(rt + 1) * (S[b] + 1)}"
                  f" <= (rt+1)2^{b}={(rt + 1) * 2 ** b}")

    banner("4. Averaging normal form: some a-set of coordinates gives <= aL/n turns")
    for n in (5, 6):
        tr = records[n]
        L = len(tr)
        prof = flip_profile(tr, n)
        print(f"  n={n}, L={L}, flip profile={prof}, sum={sum(prof)}")
        for a in range(1, n):
            R, t = best_row_set(tr, n, a)
            assert t * n <= a * L
            print(f"     a={a}: best row set {R} has {t} turns  <=  aL/n = {a * L / n:.2f}")

    banner("5. A one-turn comb in Q_7 built from two snakes of Q_6")
    A6 = records[6]
    best_total, bestA, bestB = -1, [], []
    for A in (A6[1:], A6[::-1][1:], A6):
        B = one_turn_comb(A, 6, time_limit=8)
        if len(A) + len(B) + 1 > best_total:
            best_total, bestA, bestB = len(A) + len(B) + 1, list(A), B
    tr7 = bestA + [6] + bestB
    verts7 = vertices_from_transitions(tr7)
    assert is_snake(verts7)
    prof7 = flip_profile(tr7, 7)
    print(f"  snake in Q_7 of length {len(tr7)}  = {len(bestA)} + 1 + {len(bestB)}")
    print(f"  flip profile = {prof7}  (coordinate 6 flips exactly once)")
    rows7 = [project(v, [6]) for v in verts7]
    print(f"  row sequence in Q_1 x Q_6 is a comb: {is_comb(rows7)}, turns = {turn_count(rows7)}")
    S[7] = len(tr7)
    records[7] = tr7

    banner("6. Comb saturation: does min-flip meet ceil((L+1)/(S(n-1)+1)) - 1 ?")
    print("   (S(n-1) taken as the known maximum; S(6) = 26)")
    exact = {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 4, 4: 7, 5: 13, 6: 26}
    for n in range(2, 8):
        tr = records[n]
        L = len(tr)
        prof = flip_profile(tr, n)
        lower = math.ceil((L + 1) / (exact[n - 1] + 1)) - 1
        mn = min(prof)
        print(f"  n={n}: L={L:2d}  min flip={mn}  lower bound={lower}  "
              f"averaging bound floor(L/n)={L // n}  saturated={mn == lower}")

    print("\nAll assertions passed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

        return not any((w ^ (1 << j)) in on and (w ^ (1 << j)) != v for j in range(m))

    def rec(path: List[int], on: set, tr: List[int]) -> None:
        nonlocal best
        if len(tr) > len(best):
            best = list(tr)
        if time.time() > deadline:
            return
        v = path[-1]
        for i in range(m):
            w = v ^ (1 << i)
            if ok(w, on, v):

                rec(path, on, tr)
                path.pop(); on.discard(w); tr.pop()

def turn_minimal_split(trans: Sequence[int], n: int, a: int) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int], int]:

function popc(x){ let c=0; while(x){ c+=x&1; x>>=1;} return c; }

  "interactive_layout": "# How Often Must a Snake Turn?

*A guided tour of turn-minimal normal forms for snakes in the hypercube.*

## 1. The game

The $n$-dimensional hypercube $Q_n$ has the $2^n$ bit strings of length $n$ as its corners. Two corners are joined when they differ in exactly one bit. A **snake** is a path along edges that never comes back next to itself: each new corner is adjacent to the previous corner and to no other corner already visited. The [snake-in-the-box problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake-in-the-box) asks for the longest snake, $S(n)$. The values are known only up to $n = 7$:

| $n$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $S(n)$ | 1 | 2 | 4 | 7 | 13 | 26 | 50 |

<details><summary>Formal definition of a snake</summary>

A map $p:\mathbb{N}\to V$ is a *snake in $G$ on the window $[a,b]$* if $p$ is injective on $[a,b]$ and, for all $i,j\in[a,b]$, $p_i \sim p_j \iff |i-j| = 1$. A snake of length $L$ is a snake on $[0,L]$: it has $L$ edges and $L+1$ vertices. A *snake bound* for $G$ is a number $S$ with $b - a \le S$ for every snake on every window. Since a snake visits distinct vertices, $|V|-1$ is always a snake bound.
</details>

## 2. Rows, columns and turns

Split the $n$ bits into $a$ **row bits** and $b = n-a$ **column bits**. This identifies $Q_n$ with the [box (Cartesian) product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product_of_graphs) $Q_a \,\square\, Q_b$. Each step of a snake flips one bit, so it moves either within its row or to a new row. A step of the second kind is a **turn**. Between turns the snake crawls through a **block**.

The first fact is pure bookkeeping:

> **Step accounting.** For every walk in $G\,\square\,H$: (row turns) $+$ (column turns) $=$ length.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>

An edge of $G\,\square\,H$ is either a $G$-edge with equal $H$-coordinates or an $H$-edge with equal $G$-coordinates. Each step therefore increments exactly one of the two counters. Induct on the length.
</details>

## 3. Combs are exactly the turn-minimal sequences

Play with row sequences below. Type letters, watch the turns (white bars), and press *Comb-ify*.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **Comb Theorem.** A row sequence visiting $r$ distinct rows makes at least $r-1$ turns, with equality if and only if it is a **comb**, meaning every row occupies one contiguous block.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>

Cutting at the $t$ turns leaves $t+1$ maximal blocks. Each row owns at least one block, so $t+1 \ge r$. Equality holds iff each row owns exactly one block, which is the comb condition.
</details>

## 4. Snakes are forced to turn

Inside a block the row is constant, so the snake lives in one copy of $Q_b$, and the snake rule still applies there.

> **Block Lemma.** Every block of a snake in $G\,\square\,H$ is a snake in $H$.
>
> **Direction changes are essential.** If every snake of $H$ has length $\le S$, a snake of length $L$ in $G\,\square\,H$ with $t$ turns satisfies $$L+1 \le (t+1)(S+1).$$ In $Q_{a+b}$, unconditionally, $L + 1 \le (t+1)\,2^b$.

<details><summary>Proof sketch</summary>

For corners in the same row, $(g,h)\sim(g,h')$ iff $h\sim_H h'$, because $g \sim g$ is impossible. So injectivity and induced adjacency pass to the column sequence of a block. There are $t+1$ blocks, each with at most $S+1$ corners, and together they cover all $L+1$ corners. The hypercube version uses the fact that $\mathrm{split}: Q_{a+b}\to Q_a\,\square\,Q_b$ preserves and reflects adjacency, because Hamming distance adds over the two coordinate blocks. It also uses the trivial snake bound $2^b - 1$.
</details>

## 5. ...but they never have to turn often

Every step flips exactly one coordinate, so the **flip profile** (how often each bit flips) sums to $L$. Choosing the least-flipped bits as the row gives few turns. Relabelling coordinates is a symmetry of $Q_n$, so the snake keeps its full length.

> **Averaging Normal Form.** For every snake of length $L$ in $Q_n$ and every $1\le a\le n$, after a coordinate permutation (which preserves the length exactly), the split $Q_a\,\square\,Q_{n-a}$ has
> $$\frac{L+1}{2^{n-a}} - 1 \;\le\; t \;\le\; \frac{aL}{n}.$$

<details><summary>Proof</summary>

The row sequence for row set $R$ changes exactly when the flipped bit lies in $R$, so $t_R = \sum_{i\in R}\varphi_i$. Summing over all $a$-sets gives $\sum_R t_R = \binom{n-1}{a-1}L$, so the average is $aL/n$, and the $a$ least-flipped bits do at least as well. The lower bound is the Block Lemma bound from Section 4.
</details>

For $a = 1$ this is the conjectured "$O(L/n)$ direction changes", with **zero** loss of length instead of the hoped-for $O(n)$. Explore it yourself: load a record snake, toggle the row bits, and press the auto-pick button.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Here is the same computation as a short routine:

{{algorithm:0}}

## 6. True but cheap

The averaging bound holds for *every* snake, good or bad, so by itself it cannot shrink a search space. The bound that carries information is the lower one, which comes from the Block Lemma. A useful normal form should push snakes toward that end, which means requiring **long blocks**. That is the open problem.

## 7. What the records look like

Run the full numerical companion. It searches for records with $n\le 6$, checks step accounting and the Block Lemma on every split with $a \in\{1,2\}$, verifies the averaging bound for every $a$, builds a one-turn comb in $Q_7$, and tests comb saturation.

{{demo:0}}

The search engine behind it:

{{algorithm:1}}

And the construction of one-turn combs, two snakes of $Q_{n-1}$ joined by a single hop:

{{algorithm:2}}

{{visualization:0}}

Two patterns stand out:

* the least-flipped coordinate meets the forced lower bound $\lceil (L+1)/(S(n-1)+1)\rceil - 1 = 1$ at $n = 2,3,4,5,7$; the only exception is the $26$-snake at $n=6$;
* it is flipped at most $L/(2n)$ times in each record with $n \ge 5$, half the averaging guarantee.

<details><summary>Open conjectures suggested by the data</summary>

1. **Comb saturation:** some longest snake meets the turn lower bound $\lceil (S(n)+1)/(S(n-a)+1)\rceil-1$ in some split.
2. **One-turn doubling gap:** $S(n)\ge 2S(n-1)-c$ via one-turn combs.
3. **Uneven flip profile:** $\min_i\varphi_i \le L/(2n)$ for longest snakes, $n\ge 5$.
4. **Block-maximal normal form:** at cost $O(n)$, all but $O(1)$ blocks have length $\ge S(n-1)/2$.
</details>

Further reading: [Snake-in-the-box on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake-in-the-box), [Hypercube graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercube_graph), [Gray codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gray_code).

/-!
# Snakes in product graphs and the turn lower bound

A *snake* (induced path) in a graph `G` on the index window `[a, b]` is a map
`p : ℕ → V` that is injective on `[a, b]` and such that `p i, p j` are adjacent
exactly when `|i - j| = 1`.  The hypercube splits as a box product
`Q_{m+k} ≅ Q_m □ Q_k`, so a snake in `Q_n` is a snake in a product `G □ H`; its
*row sequence* is the `G`-coordinate.

Main results:

* `TurnMinimal.turnCount_row_add_turnCount_col`: for any walk in `G □ H`,
  `#row changes + #column changes = length` (every step moves in exactly one factor);
* `TurnMinimal.IsSnakeOn.column_of_row_const`: a row block of a product snake is a snake
  in the column factor `H`;
* `TurnMinimal.succ_le_turnCount_succ_mul`: **direction changes are essential** —
  if every snake in `H` has length at most `S`, a snake of length `L` in `G □ H` satisfies
  `L + 1 ≤ (turnCount + 1) * (S + 1)`.
-/

namespace TurnMinimal

variable {V W : Type*}

/-- `p` is a snake (induced path) in `G` on the index window `[a, b]`. -/
def IsSnakeOn (G : SimpleGraph V) (p : ℕ → V) (a b : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (∀ i j, a ≤ i → i ≤ b → a ≤ j → j ≤ b → p i = p j → i = j) ∧
  (∀ i j, a ≤ i → i ≤ b → a ≤ j → j ≤ b → (G.Adj (p i) (p j) ↔ (i + 1 = j ∨ j + 1 = i)))

/-- A snake of length `L` (starting at index `0`). -/
def IsSnake (G : SimpleGraph V) (p : ℕ → V) (L : ℕ) : Prop := IsSnakeOn G p 0 L

/-- Every snake in `G` has length (number of edges) at most `S`. -/
def SnakeBound (G : SimpleGraph V) (S : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ (p : ℕ → V) (a b : ℕ), a ≤ b → IsSnakeOn G p a b → b - a ≤ S

/-- `p` is a walk of length `L`: consecutive vertices are adjacent. -/
def IsWalk (G : SimpleGraph V) (p : ℕ → V) (L : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ s, s < L → G.Adj (p s) (p (s + 1))

lemma IsSnake.isWalk {G : SimpleGraph V} {p : ℕ → V} {L : ℕ} (h : IsSnake G p L) :
    IsWalk G p L := fun s hs =>
  (h.2 s (s + 1) (Nat.zero_le _) hs.le (Nat.zero_le _) hs).2 (Or.inl rfl)

/-- **Step accounting.** Every step of a walk in `G □ H` changes exactly one coordinate,
so the row changes and the column changes add up to the length. -/
theorem turnCount_row_add_turnCount_col [DecidableEq V] [DecidableEq W]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} {p : ℕ → V × W} {L : ℕ}
    (hw : IsWalk (G □ H) p L) :
    turnCount (fun s => (p s).1) L + turnCount (fun s => (p s).2) L = L := by
  induction L with
  | zero => simp [turnCount_zero]
  | succ L ih =>
    have ih := ih (fun s hs => hw s (by omega))
    rw [turnCount_succ, turnCount_succ]
    have hadj := hw L (by omega)
    rw [SimpleGraph.boxProd_adj] at hadj
    rcases hadj with ⟨hG, hc⟩ | ⟨hH, hr⟩

# The hypercube as a box product, and turn bounds for snakes in `Q_n`

`Q n` is the `n`-dimensional hypercube on `Fin n → Bool` (adjacent iff Hamming distance `1`).
Splitting coordinates as `Fin (a + b) = Fin a ⊕ Fin b` embeds `Q (a + b)` into the box product
`Q a □ Q b` isomorphically on adjacency.  Consequently, for any snake in `Q (a + b)`:

* `TurnMinimal.hypercube_rowTurns_add_colTurns`: (flips among the first `a` coordinates) +
  (flips among the last `b` coordinates) = length;
* `TurnMinimal.hypercube_succ_le_turns_mul`: if every snake in `Q b` has length `≤ S`, then
  `L + 1 ≤ (rowTurns + 1) * (S + 1)`;
* `TurnMinimal.hypercube_succ_le_turns_mul_pow`: unconditionally,
  `L + 1 ≤ (rowTurns + 1) * 2 ^ b`.
-/

namespace TurnMinimal

variable {V W : Type*}

/-- The `n`-dimensional hypercube graph. -/
def Q (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin n → Bool) where
  Adj x y := hammingDist x y = 1
  symm x y h := by simpa [hammingDist_comm] using h
  loopless := ⟨fun x h => by simp at h⟩

/-- Split a vertex of `Q (a + b)` into its first `a` and last `b` coordinates. -/
def split (a b : ℕ) (x : Fin (a + b) → Bool) : (Fin a → Bool) × (Fin b → Bool) :=
  (fun i => x (Fin.castAdd b i), fun j => x (Fin.natAdd a j))

lemma split_injective (a b : ℕ) : Function.Injective (split a b) := by
  intro x y h
  simp only [split, Prod.mk.injEq] at h
  funext k
  refine Fin.addCases (fun i => ?_) (fun j => ?_) k
  · exact congrFun h.1 i
  · exact congrFun h.2 j

lemma hammingDist_split (a b : ℕ) (x y : Fin (a + b) → Bool) :
    hammingDist x y = hammingDist (split a b x).1 (split a b y).1 +
      hammingDist (split a b x).2 (split a b y).2 := by
  simp only [hammingDist, split, Finset.card_filter]
  exact Fin.sum_univ_add (fun k => if x k ≠ y k then 1 else 0)

/-- The coordinate split is a graph isomorphism `Q (a + b) ≅ Q a □ Q b` on adjacency. -/
theorem Q_adj_iff_split (a b : ℕ) (x y : Fin (a + b) → Bool) :
    (Q (a + b)).Adj x y ↔ (Q a □ Q b).Adj (split a b x) (split a b y) := by
  change hammingDist x y = 1 ↔ _
  rw [SimpleGraph.boxProd_adj, hammingDist_split]
  change _ ↔ (hammingDist _ _ = 1 ∧ _) ∨ (hammingDist _ _ = 1 ∧ _)
  constructor
  · intro h
    rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos (hammingDist (split a b x).1 (split a b y).1) with h0 | h0
    · exact Or.inr ⟨by omega, hammingDist_eq_zero.1 h0⟩
    · exact Or.inl ⟨by omega, hammingDist_eq_zero.1 (by omega)⟩
  · rintro (⟨h1, h2⟩ | ⟨h1, h2⟩)
    · rw [h1, h2, hammingDist_self]
    · rw [h1, h2, hammingDist_self]

theorem IsSnakeOn.map {G : SimpleGraph V} {G' : SimpleGraph W} {f : V → W}
    (hf : Function.Injective f) (hadj : ∀ x y, G.Adj x y ↔ G'.Adj (f x) (f y))
    {p : ℕ → V} {a b : ℕ} (h : IsSnakeOn G p a b) : IsSnakeOn G' (fun i => f (p i)) a b :=
  ⟨fun i j hai hib haj hjb hij => h.1 i j hai hib haj hjb (hf hij),
   fun i j hai hib haj hjb => (hadj _ _).symm.trans (h.2 i j hai hib haj hjb)⟩

    intro i hi j hj hij
    simp only [Finset.coe_Icc, Set.mem_Icc] at hi hj
    exact h.1 i j hi.1 hi.2 hj.1 hj.2 hij

  rw [Finset.card_image_of_injOn hinj, Nat.card_Icc] at this
  omega

theorem hypercube_rowTurns_add_colTurns {a b L : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Fin (a + b) → Bool}

theorem hypercube_succ_le_turns_mul {a b L S : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Fin (a + b) → Bool}
    (hp : IsSnake (Q (a + b)) p L) (hS : SnakeBound (Q b) S) :
    L + 1 ≤ (turnCount (fun s => (split a b (p s)).1) L + 1) * (S + 1) := by
  have h' : IsSnake (Q a □ Q b) (fun s => split a b (p s)) L :=
    IsSnakeOn.map (split_injective a b) (Q_adj_iff_split a b) hp
  exact succ_le_turnCount_succ_mul h' hS

/-- Unconditional version: `L + 1 ≤ (rowTurns + 1) * 2 ^ b`. -/
theorem hypercube_succ_le_turns_mul_pow {a b L : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Fin (a + b) → Bool}

    L + 1 ≤ (turnCount (fun s => (split a b (p s)).1) L + 1) * 2 ^ b := by
  have h := hypercube_succ_le_turns_mul hp (snakeBound_card (Q b))
  have hc : Fintype.card (Fin b → Bool) = 2 ^ b := by simp
  rw [hc, Nat.sub_add_cancel (Nat.one_le_two_pow)] at h
  exact h

/-!
# Turn counts of row sequences and minimality of the comb

A path in a product `G □ H` determines a *row sequence* `row : ℕ → α`
(its first coordinate).  The *turn count* of the path on `[0, L]` is the number of
steps `s < L` at which the row changes.  We prove:

* `TurnMinimal.card_rows_le_turnCount_succ`: a path visiting `r` distinct rows makes at
  least `r - 1` turns;
* `TurnMinimal.IsComb.turnCount_succ_eq`: the comb (each row visited in one contiguous
  block) attains this minimum exactly;
* `TurnMinimal.isComb_iff_turnCount_succ_eq`: conversely the comb is the *only* minimiser.
-/

namespace TurnMinimal

variable {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]

/-- Number of steps `s < L` at which the row sequence changes. -/
def turnCount (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.range L).filter (fun s => row s ≠ row (s + 1))).card

/-- Set of rows visited on `[0, L]`. -/
def rowSet (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) : Finset α :=
  (Finset.range (L + 1)).image row

/-- Comb property: every row is visited in a single contiguous block of times. -/
def IsComb (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j k, i ≤ j → j ≤ k → k ≤ L → row i = row k → row j = row i

lemma turnCount_zero (row : ℕ → α) : turnCount row 0 = 0 := by
  simp [turnCount]

lemma turnCount_succ (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) :
    turnCount row (L + 1) = turnCount row L + if row L ≠ row (L + 1) then 1 else 0 := by
  unfold turnCount
  rw [Finset.range_add_one, Finset.filter_insert]
  split_ifs with h
  · rw [Finset.card_insert_of_notMem (by simp)]
  · rfl

lemma rowSet_succ (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) :
    rowSet row (L + 1) = insert (row (L + 1)) (rowSet row L) := by
  unfold rowSet
  rw [Finset.range_add_one (n := L + 1), Finset.image_insert]

lemma mem_rowSet {row : ℕ → α} {L : ℕ} {a : α} :
    a ∈ rowSet row L ↔ ∃ i ≤ L, row i = a := by
  simp [rowSet]

lemma turnCount_le (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) : turnCount row L ≤ L := by
  unfold turnCount
  exact (Finset.card_filter_le _ _).trans (by simp)

theorem card_rows_le_turnCount_succ (row : ℕ → α) (L : ℕ) :
    (rowSet row L).card ≤ turnCount row L + 1 := by
  induction L with
  | zero => simp [rowSet, turnCount_zero]
  | succ L ih =>
    rw [rowSet_succ, turnCount_succ]
    by_cases h : row L = row (L + 1)
    · have : row (L + 1) ∈ rowSet row L := mem_rowSet.2 ⟨L, le_rfl, h⟩
      rw [Finset.insert_eq_of_mem this]
      simp [h, ih]
    · have := Finset.card_insert_le (row (L + 1)) (rowSet row L)
      simp only [ne_eq, h, not_false_eq_true, if_true]
      omega

lemma IsComb.mono {row : ℕ → α} {L M : ℕ} (h : IsComb row L) (hM : M ≤ L) :

        simp only [hL, ne_eq, not_true_eq_false, if_false] at heq
        exact ⟨by omega, fun h => absurd hL h⟩
      · simp only [ne_eq, hL, not_false_eq_true, if_true] at heq

        rw [Finset.insert_eq_of_mem hm] at heq

        have : j = L + 1 := by omega

theorem IsComb.turnCount_le_of_rowSet_eq {row row' : ℕ → α} {L L' : ℕ}
    (h : IsComb row L) (hrows : rowSet row L = rowSet row' L') :

/-!
# Turn-minimal normal form in the split `Q_n = Q_1 □ Q_{n-1}`

For a snake `p` in `Q n` and a coordinate `i`, the *flip count* `flips p L i` is the turn count
of the row sequence `s ↦ p s i`, i.e. the number of direction changes of `p` viewed as a product
snake in `Q_1 □ Q_{n-1}` with row coordinate `i`.

* `TurnMinimal.sum_flips_eq`: the flip counts of all coordinates add up to the length `L`;
* `TurnMinimal.exists_flips_le`: some coordinate is flipped at most `L / n` times;
* `TurnMinimal.flips_lower_bound`: every coordinate is flipped at least
  `(L + 1) / (S + 1) - 1` times, where `S` bounds snakes in `Q_{n-1}`;
* `TurnMinimal.turn_normal_form`: **normal form** — every snake of length `L` in `Q_{1+b}`
  becomes, after relabelling coordinates (a hypercube automorphism, so with *no* loss of length),
  a product snake in `Q_1 □ Q_b` with at most `L / (1 + b)` direction changes, and no product
  decomposition can do better than `(L + 1) / (S + 1) - 1`.
-/

namespace TurnMinimal

/-- Number of steps `s < L` of `p` flipping coordinate `i`. -/
def flips {n : ℕ} (p : ℕ → Fin n → Bool) (L : ℕ) (i : Fin n) : ℕ :=
  turnCount (fun s => p s i) L

/-- Each step of a hypercube walk flips exactly one coordinate, so the flip counts sum to `L`. -/
theorem sum_flips_eq {n L : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Fin n → Bool} (hw : IsWalk (Q n) p L) :
    ∑ i, flips p L i = L := by
  have hstep : ∀ s ∈ Finset.range L,
      ∑ i : Fin n, (if p s i ≠ p (s + 1) i then 1 else 0) = 1 := by
    intro s hs
    have h := hw s (Finset.mem_range.1 hs)
    change hammingDist (p s) (p (s + 1)) = 1 at h
    rw [hammingDist, Finset.card_filter] at h
    exact h
  calc ∑ i, flips p L i
      = ∑ i : Fin n, ∑ s ∈ Finset.range L, (if p s i ≠ p (s + 1) i then 1 else 0) := by
        simp only [flips, turnCount, Finset.card_filter]
    _ = ∑ s ∈ Finset.range L, ∑ i : Fin n, (if p s i ≠ p (s + 1) i then 1 else 0) :=
        Finset.sum_comm
    _ = ∑ s ∈ Finset.range L, 1 := Finset.sum_congr rfl hstep
    _ = L := by simp

/-- Pigeonhole: some coordinate is flipped at most `L / n` times. -/
theorem exists_flips_le {n L : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) {p : ℕ → Fin n → Bool}
    (hw : IsWalk (Q n) p L) : ∃ i, n * flips p L i ≤ L := by
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  have hsum := sum_flips_eq hw
  have : ∑ _i : Fin n, L < ∑ i, n * flips p L i :=
    Finset.sum_lt_sum_of_nonempty ⟨⟨0, hn⟩, Finset.mem_univ _⟩ (fun i _ => hcon i)
  rw [← Finset.mul_sum, hsum] at this
  simp at this

/-- Hamming distance is invariant under relabelling coordinates. -/
lemma hammingDist_comp_perm {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (x y : Fin n → Bool) :
    hammingDist (x ∘ σ) (y ∘ σ) = hammingDist x y := by
  simp only [hammingDist, Finset.card_filter, Function.comp]
  exact Equiv.sum_comp σ (fun k => if x k ≠ y k then 1 else 0)

/-- Relabelling coordinates is an automorphism of `Q n`. -/
lemma Q_adj_comp_perm {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (x y : Fin n → Bool) :
    (Q n).Adj x y ↔ (Q n).Adj (x ∘ σ) (y ∘ σ) := by
  change _ = 1 ↔ _ = 1
  rw [hammingDist_comp_perm]

lemma comp_perm_injective {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    Function.Injective (fun x : Fin n → Bool => x ∘ σ) := by
  intro x y h
  funext k
  simpa using congrFun h (σ.symm k)

theorem flips_lower_bound {b L S : ℕ} {p : ℕ → Fin (1 + b) → Bool}

    ∃ i, (1 + b) * flips p L i ≤ L ∧ L + 1 ≤ (flips p L i + 1) * (S + 1) := by
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ := exists_flips_le (by omega) hp.isWalk
  exact ⟨i, hi, flips_lower_bound hp hS i⟩
